transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2027-08-10 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Ortega (Redwood SE), Asha Kapoor (Head of Platform, BrynnCore), Tom Reyes (CTO), Nina Patel (Procurement)

Auto-generated Summary: BrynnCore is evaluating a mid-contract top-up to cover anticipated Q4 traffic surge and wants to accelerate an EU private pilot (VPC) to meet data residency requirements. Primary asks: clear pricing for a 6-month amortized uplift, timeline for private VPC activation, and a short stress test to validate latency at peak. Redwood to deliver updated pricing + run test.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everybody, thanks for jumping on. Quick intro, I'm Maya from Redwood, uh, AE on the account. With me is Liam from Solutions Eng.
[00:08] Asha Kapoor: Hi Maya, hi Liam. Asha here. Thanks — we've got Tom and Nina on as well, so we'll cover procurement and platform.
[00:15] Tom Reyes: Yup, thanks. We wanted to lock down a path to add capacity and get EU private running before end of Q3.
[00:22] Maya Chen: Great. Goal for today: walk through proposal for top-up, timing for VPC/private, and call out any contract asks.
[00:30] Liam Ortega: I'll surface what the stress tests will look like and what telemetry we'll need from you to get accurate latency/throughput numbers.
[00:36] Asha Kapoor: Cool. We also wanted to compare a short-term burst vs reserved uplift — cost and SLA tradeoffs.
[00:43] Nina Patel: And from procurement, we'll need the amendment language and PO details.
[00:47] Maya Chen: Absolutely. Quick note — I'll be sharing a revised pricing sheet after the call with amortized payments for the 6-month top-up and the EU pilot SOW.
[00:55] Tom Reyes: Perfect. So to frame it: our internal traffic projection shows ~2.2x in peak tokens per minute during holiday promos. Today we're on a Dedicated mid-tier commit and hitting queueing around 180ms p50, 420ms p95. We want to keep p95 under 400ms if possible.
[01:15] Liam Ortega: Okay, that's helpful. Are those numbers coming from our instrumented SDK or internal load generator?
[01:20] Tom Reyes: Internal load generator + some synthetic from staging. We saw KV cache misses spike during longer context flows, so there may be prefix cache warmup issues.
[01:29] Liam Ortega: Right, KV cache warmup is a common cause — sometimes the K-V cash, ha, gets cold. We can run a test to exercise prefix caching. For the EU private, we'll want a short canary to validate cross-region hops if you plan to fallback to hosted in the interim.
[01:45] Asha Kapoor: Our legal requires data residency for EU customer content; we can't route anything outside EU during the pilot. So private VPC is actually a hard requirement for that subset of traffic.
[01:55] Maya Chen: Understood. We can support VPC activation with customer-managed transit in AZ/eu-west-1 region. Typical surface area: VPC peering or PrivateLink, KMS integration for key wrap, and audit logs forwarded to your SIEM.
[02:10] Nina Patel: Do you have SOC 2 + ISO artifacts ready? We need them for procurement.
[02:15] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll attach current SOC 2 Type II and ISO documentation. Also note the audit logs can be tailored for retention durations.
[02:22] Tom Reyes: On latency, if we do a dedicated top-up vs burst, what's the typical improvement? Like ballpark p95 drop?
[02:29] Liam Ortega: Ballpark — moving from a mid-tier commit to a top-up of an additional 4x vGPU capacity reduces queueing and gives us headroom; you'd likely see p95 improve from 420ms to around 300–350ms depending on sequence lengths. But the exact number depends on batching profiles and quantization profiles for the model variant you're on.
[02:46] Asha Kapoor: What's the timeline to provision EU private? If we sign the amendment this week can we get staging in two weeks?
[02:52] Maya Chen: For a standard EU private VPC activation we usually do: 1) Provisioning and network handoff (3–5 business days), 2) KMS and cert exchange (2–3 days), 3) staging validation and canary (3–5 days). So optimistic 8–13 business days. If we overlap tasks we might hit two weeks.
[03:12] Nina Patel: That fits our internal cadence. Procurement wants a 6-month amendment, not monthly. We prefer amortized billing and a termination clause for non-delivery of SLA.
[03:22] Maya Chen: We can draft an amendment with a 6-month commit for the top-up and EU pilot, include SLOs and an SLA credit formula. We'll send a draft.
[03:29] Tom Reyes: On failure modes, what's Redwood's fallback? If EU capacity saturates, do you route to hosted fallback outside EU? We can't allow that for regulated traffic.
[03:38] Liam Ortega: For traffic flagged as residency-sensitive, we'll maintain strict routing to EU-resident nodes. If capacity is exhausted, we can queue or return a 429 depending on your preference. We can also set up a circuit-breaker and a retry window so that non-sensitive traffic can fallback to hosted to preserve availability.
[03:55] Asha Kapoor: Good. We'll need the retry/circuit-breaker behavior documented in the runbook.
[03:59] Liam Ortega: Noted.
[04:02] Maya Chen: Let's talk numbers — we've modeled 4 extra gpus dedicated to EU for initial pilot (we can language it as 4 x A100-equivalent). Pricing options: burst/usage-based (higher unit cost), 6-month amortized reserved top-up (lower effective unit cost), or a hybrid where you buy committed nodes with burst overlay.
[04:22] Nina Patel: Are there volume discounts if we convert this top-up into a permanent uplift at renewal?
[04:27] Maya Chen: Yes, we can include stepdown discounts if you convert the top-up into the annual commit at renewal; we'll show that in the spreadsheet.
[04:34] Tom Reyes: For the stress test, what's the observed token-per-second per GPU for the model we're using? We're on the 'redwood-pegasus-13b' variant, right?
[04:42] Liam Ortega: You're on a 13B-ish open variant. For light quantization and normal sequence lengths (avg 220 tokens) you should see roughly 1800–2500 tokens/sec per GPU with our optimized kernels. But again that swings with context length and attention patterns. We'll test with your real traces.
[05:01] Asha Kapoor: We'll share a scrubbed week of traffic patterns — are there any format requirements?
[05:06] Liam Ortega: JSON lines with timestamp, route, sequence length, and sample outputs is ideal. We can accept anonymized payloads. Send via the secure upload link in the SOW.
[05:15] Nina Patel: Any security caveat to sharing traces?
[05:18] Maya Chen: We'll sign an NDA addendum for the trace set and you can also encrypt at rest. For the pilot we recommend using synthetic but representative traces.
[05:26] Tom Reyes: Ok. About failover again — what's the policy during maintenance windows? We run rolling updates, how much downtime should we expect?
[05:33] Liam Ortega: For Dedicated and Private, rolling deploys normally keep you online; planned maintenance is usually sub-1% of traffic with graceful drain. We'll share maintenance windows up-front and you can configure hard cutover times.
[05:44] Asha Kapoor: Sounds good. Can you also include model-version pinning in the amendment so we don't get surprise regressions?
[05:49] Maya Chen: Yes — we'll include version pinning and a controlled rollout policy for model upgrades (canary percent, QA gate).
[05:55] Tom Reyes: Let's fast forward to procurement questions — Nina?
[05:58] Nina Patel: Two asks: 1) PO/contract template; 2) SLA metrics clearly spelled out and credits calculation. Also, can you confirm KMS integration options — we prefer HSM-backed keys.
[06:09] Maya Chen: We'll attach PO language and an SLA appendix. KMS: we support customer-managed KMS and HSM-backed keys via our KMS integration (we'll send integration doc).
[06:18] Nina Patel: Great. On billing cadence — we want to do monthly amortized invoices for the 6-month uplift to align with forecasting.
[06:24] Maya Chen: That's the default for amortized top-ups. We'll show the amortization in the spreadsheet.
[06:28] Tom Reyes: Any limitations with the EU private environment on streaming APIs and function calling? We rely heavily on streaming tokens to UI.
[06:35] Liam Ortega: Streaming and function/tool call patterns are supported in Private exactly like hosted — but there is an extra 10–20ms due to VPC routing in some cases. We'll measure this in the canary.
[06:47] Asha Kapoor: Are there any special observability hooks we can enable? We want per-route token cost breakdown in our SLO dashboard.
[06:54] Maya Chen: Yes — we can enable per-route token accounting and emit telemetry to your Prometheus endpoint or forward traces to your tracing solution. We'll include connectors in the runbook.
[07:05] Tom Reyes: On commitment sizing — we're leaning toward 4 extra GPUs for two months then scale to 8 for Q4 peak. How does that work operationally?
[07:13] Liam Ortega: We can stage the increase: provision initial 4 node pool in EU, and then pre-reserve an additional capacity buffer that we can activate within 24–48 hours during the ramp. That buffer is usually cheaper if reserved ahead of time.
[07:28] Nina Patel: If we need to cancel the second activation, what's the penalty?
[07:31] Maya Chen: We'll include a cancellation window in the SOW — typically a 30-day notice to avoid charges on reserved activations. We'll detail that.
[07:38] Asha Kapoor: Quick technical — does Redwood support custom kernel flags for the compiled runtime? We have a few bespoke attention patterns.
[07:45] Liam Ortega: We do support tunable kernel settings for private customers, but it requires additional validation and may affect support SLAs. We can share technical notes; if you need it, discuss with our research team during the pilot.
[07:58] Tom Reyes: Okay. Anything else on tech?
[08:00] Asha Kapoor: Not right now. Let's get to the test plan. Liam, walk us through the 72-hour stress test.
[08:06] Liam Ortega: Sure. Phase 1: baseline validation (4 hours) to check routes and KMS. Phase 2: ramping load over 24 hours to 1.5x expected peak. Phase 3: sustained 48-hour window at 2x expected peak with randomized sequences and prefix cache cold starts injected. We'll collect p50/p95/p99 latencies, GPU utilization, batch sizes, and cache hit rates. We'll provide dashboards and raw logs.
[08:30] Tom Reyes: That sounds thorough. For the prefix cold starts — will you simulate different user sessions?
[08:34] Liam Ortega: Yes, we'll feed unique sessions and prefixes to force KV misses. We'll also measure how caching warms up over the sustained window.
[08:42] Asha Kapoor: Will the test traffic be routed through our EU private nodes only?
[08:46] Liam Ortega: For the pilot test we'll isolate traffic to the EU pool. We can do a cross-check test with hosted fallback to measure differences.
[08:54] Nina Patel: For reporting, can we get a one-pager with pass/fail criteria? Procurement likes binary outcomes.
[09:00] Maya Chen: Yes — we'll produce a one-page runbook with pass/fail thresholds and risk items.
[09:06] Tom Reyes: On the SRE side, do you support on-call integration and paging? We want alerts sent to PagerDuty.
[09:12] Liam Ortega: We can push alerts to PagerDuty, Opsgenie, or Slack channels. We'll include runbook alerts and thresholds.
[09:20] Asha Kapoor: Okay, let's talk timeline — if we get the SOW and sign by Friday, can the staging VPC be up by two weeks?
[09:27] Maya Chen: Yes, that's the target. We'll prioritize provisioning.
[09:30] Nina Patel: One minor question — do you have any pre-approved vendor forms we need to fill? Our legal uses a redline-first flow.
[09:36] Maya Chen: We can accept redlines; we'll have our legal coordinate. We'll include a quick checklist of common redline items to speed review.
[09:44] Tom Reyes: Competitors check — we ran a quick bake-off vs CumulusAI last month and saw comparable latency, but their observability was weaker. Any nuances we should be aware of in terms of region activation latency?
[09:56] Liam Ortega: Cumulus tends to use different batching heuristics; some of the variance you saw could be from different KV cache strategies. We can try to replicate their workload to show delta. Infera Labs is cheaper at burst but lacks private VPC options at scale.
[10:12] Asha Kapoor: Good to know.
[10:15] Maya Chen: Alright — I'll summarize and then we'll do a quick Q&A. Summary: Redwood will send revised pricing with amortized 6-month top-up and EU SOW; run a 72-hour stress test isolated to EU private nodes; provide SOC2/ISO artifacts and KMS integration doc; draft amendment with SLOs and cancellation windows; schedule runbook walkthrough.
[10:36] Tom Reyes: Perfect. Quick clarifying Q — the amortized invoice, will it show line items for committed vs burst usage?
[10:42] Maya Chen: Yes we'll break out committed nodes, burst overlay, and per-token usage if any.
[10:48] Nina Patel: Nina again — please include insurance and liability limits in the contract appendix.
[10:52] Maya Chen: We'll include standard indemnity and liability terms.
[10:56] Asha Kapoor: One last tech ask — can we get a sample canary playbook with traffic percentages and rollback triggers?
[11:02] Liam Ortega: Yes — we'll include a canary playbook template (5/20/100 rollout, rollback thresholds defined by p95 and error rate).
[11:12] Tom Reyes: That helps. Anything else?
[11:15] Nina Patel: No, that's it from procurement.
[11:18] Maya Chen: Great. We'll follow up with the docs and SOW. Thanks everyone.
[11:22] Asha Kapoor: Thanks all.
[11:24] End of call.

Notes on transcript quality: There are a few auto-corrections (K-V cash for KV cache), and occasional attribution errors; filler words left intact.
notes: Customer explicitly requires EU-residency for a subset of traffic — private VPC mandatory for that scope
Redwood to provide amortized pricing for 6-month top-up and SOW for EU pilot
72-hour stress test scope agreed; customer to provide anonymized traces
